You've given him an artificial sense of dignity and spirit, ma'am, quite unsuitable for someone in his position, as the board will tell you, Mrs. Sowerberry. They are practical philosophers. What business have paupers with dignity or spirit? It's quite enough that we allow them living bodies. If you had kept the boy on gruel, ma'am, none of this would have happened.”

“Dear, dear!” exclaimed Mrs. Sowerberry, piously lifting her eyes to the kitchen ceiling. “This is what generosity leads to!”

Mrs. Sowerberry's generosity to Oliver had consisted of lavishing upon him all the filthy scraps that nobody else would eat. There was therefore considerable humility and self-sacrifice in her willingness to accept Mr. Bumble's serious accusation, of which, to give her her due, she was entirely innocent in thought, word, and action.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, when the lady lowered her eyes to earth again. “The only thing to do now, as far as I can see, is leave him in the cellar for a day or so, until hunger takes him down a little. Then bring him out and feed him nothing but gruel for the rest of his apprenticeship. He comes from a bad family. Excitable temperaments, Mrs. Sowerberry! The nurse and the doctor both said that his mother made her way here through hardships and pain that would have killed any properly behaved woman weeks earlier.”

At this point in Mr. Bumble's speech, Oliver caught just enough to realize they were referring to his mother, and began kicking again so violently that every other sound was drowned out. Sowerberry returned at that moment. Once the ladies had explained Oliver's offense, with whatever exaggerations they thought most likely to inflame his anger, he immediately unlocked the cellar door and hauled his rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver's clothes were torn from the beating he had received; his face was bruised and scratched, and his hair fell across his forehead. But the angry flush had not faded. When he was dragged from his prison, he glared boldly at Noah and showed no sign of fear.

“Well, aren't you a fine young fellow?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and striking him on the ear.

“He insulted my mother,” Oliver answered.

“Well, what if he did, you ungrateful little wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved everything he said, and worse.”

“She didn't,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“That's a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry burst into tears.

Those tears left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Any experienced reader will readily understand that, had he hesitated even an instant to punish Oliver severely, every established precedent in marital disputes would have condemned him as a brute, an unnatural husband, an offensive creature, a contemptible imitation of a man, and various other equally agreeable things too numerous to recount within the space of this chapter.

On the hearth lay two or three long, thick locks of gray human hair, also stained with blood, which appeared to have been torn out by the roots. On the floor were four Napoleon coins, a topaz earring, three large silver spoons, three smaller spoons of Algerian metal, and two bags containing nearly four thousand francs in gold. A chest of drawers stood in one corner, its drawers open and apparently searched, although many objects remained inside. A small iron safe was found beneath the bedding, not beneath the bed frame. It was open, with its key still in the door, and contained only a few old letters and other unimportant papers.

“No trace of Madame L'Espanaye was found here. However, an unusual amount of soot was noticed in the fireplace, prompting a search of the chimney. Horrible as it is to report, the daughter's body was dragged out headfirst, having been forced head downward a considerable distance up the narrow opening. The body was still quite warm. Examination revealed numerous abrasions, undoubtedly caused by the force used to push it up the chimney and pull it free. There were many deep scratches on the face, and dark bruises and deep fingernail marks on the throat, suggesting that the deceased had been strangled.

“After thoroughly searching every part of the house without discovering anything further, the party entered a small paved yard behind the building. There lay the older woman's body, her throat cut so completely through that her head fell off when they attempted to lift her. Both the head and the body were horribly mutilated, the latter so severely that it scarcely appeared human.

“As far as we know, there is still not the slightest clue to this terrible mystery.”

The following day's newspaper supplied these additional details.

“Regarding the tragedy in the Rue Morgue, many people have been questioned about this extraordinary and appalling affair”—the French word ‘affaire’ does not yet carry the frivolous associations it has for us—“but nothing has emerged that sheds any light on it. Below we give all the relevant testimony obtained.

“Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, states that she had known both the deceased for three years and had done their washing throughout that time. The older woman and her daughter seemed to get along well and were very affectionate toward each other. They paid extremely well. She could say nothing about their way of life or their source of income. She believed Madame L. earned her living by telling fortunes. The woman was said to have savings.”

Mary never wrote to Bath herself. The entire burden of maintaining a slow and unsatisfying exchange of letters with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Not long after breakfast, Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick arrived. They had arranged to take one last walk around Lyme together. They needed to leave for Uppercross by one o'clock, and until then they meant to stay together and spend as much time outdoors as possible.

As soon as they were all out in the street, Anne found Captain Benwick moving toward her. Their conversation the night before had encouraged him to seek her company again. They walked together for some time, discussing Mr. Scott and Lord Byron as before. They were still no more able to agree completely about the merits of either writer than any two other readers would have been. Then something caused most of the group to change places, and Anne found Captain Harville beside her instead.

“Miss Elliot,” he said quietly, “you have done a kind thing by getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he could have company like yours more often. I know that staying shut away as he does is bad for him, but what can we do? We cannot bear to part.”

“No,” Anne said, “I can easily believe that would be impossible. But perhaps in time—we know how time helps with every kind of grief. And you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend's loss is still quite recent. Only last summer, I believe.”

“Yes, that's true,” he said with a deep sigh. “Only June.”

“And perhaps he did not learn of it at once.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, having just been appointed to the Grappler. I was in Plymouth, dreading news of his arrival. He sent letters ashore, but the Grappler had orders to go to Portsmouth. The news had to reach him there, but who could tell him? I couldn't. I would as soon have been hanged from the yardarm. Nobody could do it except that good fellow.” He pointed to Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had arrived in Plymouth the week before, with no risk of her going to sea again. He took his chances with the rest. He wrote requesting leave, but traveled night and day to Portsmouth without waiting for an answer. He immediately rowed out to the Grappler and stayed with the poor fellow for a week. That's what he did, and nobody else could have saved poor James. You can imagine, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us!”

Anne had no doubt about her answer. She said as much as her own feelings allowed and as his seemed able to bear. He was too moved to continue the subject, and when he spoke again, it was about something entirely different.
